details:
**Temple Mount (Mount Moriah) and the Binding of Isaac**
The hill in Jerusalem's Old City traditionally identified with Mount Moriah, where Abraham nearly sacrificed his son Isaac before an angel stopped him and a ram appeared as a substitute (Genesis 22). In Islamic tradition the son is usually identified as Ishmael. Both Jewish Temples were built here, and today it holds the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque.

**Western Wall (Wailing Wall or Kotel)**
A surviving retaining wall built during King Herod's expansion of the Second Temple complex, and the holiest place where Jews may pray today. Visitors push written prayers into its crevices; these notes are collected twice a year, including before Rosh Hashanah, and buried on the Mount of Olives. A tunnel runs along its hidden sections, and the area called Robinson's Arch has been set aside for egalitarian and women's prayer.

**Dome of the Rock and the Foundation Stone**
A golden-domed Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount, built in the late 7th century under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. It covers the Foundation Stone, a rock that Jewish tradition places at the site of the Holy of Holies and from which the world was created. Beneath the rock is a cave called the Well of Souls.

**Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Night Journey**
Al-Aqsa, "the farthest mosque," stands on the Temple Mount and is the third-holiest site in Islam after Mecca and Medina. In the Isra and Mi'raj (Night Journey), Muhammad rode the winged steed Buraq from Mecca to this "farthest mosque" in one night and then ascended to Heaven. Worshippers perform ablutions (wudu) at a nearby fountain called al-Kas ("the Cup").

**First qibla**
The qibla is the direction Muslims face during prayer. Before it was changed to face the Kaaba in Mecca, early Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem, which Muslims also call al-Quds ("the Holy").

**First Temple (Solomon's Temple)**
The Temple built by King Solomon on Mount Moriah to house the Ark of the Covenant in its innermost room, the Holy of Holies. His father David was forbidden to build it because he was a man of war who had shed blood, and King Hiram of Tyre supplied wood for it. It was destroyed by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II in 587/586 BCE, ending the Kingdom of Judah.

**Second Temple and its destruction by Titus**
Built after the Babylonian exile under Zerubbabel and greatly expanded by Herod the Great, it was destroyed by the Roman general Titus in 70 CE during the First Jewish-Roman War. The Arch of Titus in Rome commemorates this sack of Jerusalem and depicts Romans carrying off the Temple menorah.

**"Next Year in Jerusalem"**
In Hebrew, "L'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim," a phrase expressing the hope of return to Jerusalem. It is traditionally said or sung at the end of the Passover seder and at the end of the Ne'ilah service that closes Yom Kippur.

**Tisha B'Av**
The Ninth of Av, a Jewish fast day that mourns the destruction of both the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem, as well as other tragedies in Jewish history.

**Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Calvary**
Jesus was crucified on the hill of Calvary (Golgotha) outside the city walls after being sentenced by Pontius Pilate and mocked as "King of the Jews." The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is traditionally believed to contain both the crucifixion site and his tomb. Jerusalem also contains the Cenacle, the traditional "Upper Room" of the Last Supper remembered on Maundy Thursday.

**Cleansing of the Temple**
In the Gospels, Jesus enters Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, then makes a whip of cords, overturns the tables of the money changers in the Temple, and calls it a "house of prayer." He also weeps over the city and prophesies that its enemies will leave "not one stone upon another."

**Threshing floor of Araunah**
In 2 Samuel 24, after a plague sent as punishment for his census, King David bought the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite on Mount Moriah and built an altar there. This site later became the location of Solomon's Temple.

**Hanukkah and Judas Maccabeus**
After the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, Judas Maccabeus recaptured and cleansed the Temple in Jerusalem. Hanukkah celebrates its rededication and the miracle of a single jug of oil that kept the menorah lit for eight days.

**"Jerusalem of Gold"**
In Hebrew, "Yerushalayim Shel Zahav," a famous 1967 Israeli song by Naomi Shemer. Its title comes from a Talmudic story in which Rabbi Akiva gives his wife a piece of jewelry called a "Jerusalem of gold," and the lyrics call the singer a "lyre for all your songs."

**Peter and John at the Temple and Paul's arrest**
In Acts 3, Peter and John say "silver and gold have I none" before healing a man lame from birth at the Temple's Beautiful Gate. In Acts 21, Paul is seized in the Temple and arrested in Jerusalem after paying the expenses for four men completing a vow, which included having their heads shaved.
